# Summary of the Green Party Manifesto 2005

The 2005 Green Party Manifesto presents a comprehensive vision for building a sustainable society founded on social, economic, and environmental justice. The document outlines policies across ten key areas, positioning the Greens as an alternative to mainstream Westminster parties.

## Economic Policy

The Greens argue that current economic stability relies on unsustainable resource use and wealth inequality. They propose progressive taxation reforms, including higher tax bands (50% on earnings over £50,000, 60% over £100,000), reformed Corporation Tax, and a Land Value Tax to address the concentration of land ownership. The party advocates replacing VAT with eco-taxes that reflect environmental costs of production and consumption. They support economic localisation over globalisation, opposing UK entry to the euro and promoting community banks and local currencies.

## Energy and Climate Change

Climate change is identified as the gravest environmental and economic threat. The Greens adopt the "Contraction and Convergence" framework, targeting 20% carbon dioxide reduction by 2010 and 85% by 2030. Key policies include introducing a carbon tax, increasing renewable energy to 40% by 2020, implementing a Warmer Homes Act, and closing the nuclear fuel programme. They propose creating a Cabinet-level post for climate change policy.

## Welfare Reform

The manifesto introduces the Citizen's Income—an unconditional, non-means-tested payment for all UK residents covering basic needs. This would replace most existing benefits and increase incomes for the poorest households by approximately 25%. A Citizen's Pension would provide guaranteed retirement income linked to average earnings, abolishing means-tested Pension Credit.

## Health and Education

The Greens pledge to restore NHS founding principles, opposing privatisation and Public-Private Partnerships. They would abolish prescription charges, reintroduce free dental care and eye tests, and increase health funding to the EU average (approximately £90 billion). In education, they promise to scrap tuition fees, restore maintenance grants, abolish SATs, and introduce individualised learning plans.

## Transport

Transport policy prioritises sustainable modes over private vehicles, ranking walking and cycling highest, followed by public transport, then freight, with private cars last. The Greens would return rail networks to public ownership, introduce true-cost motoring through congestion charging and fuel duty increases, and tackle aviation growth through fuel taxation.

## Environmental Protection

A Zero Waste Strategy forms the centrepiece of environmental policy, aiming for 60% domestic waste recycling by 2010. The party opposes genetic modification, supports animal rights legislation, and would establish an Environmental Protection Commission to integrate research on public health and environmental protection.

## Food and Farming

The Greens propose an Organics Target Bill for 30% organic production by 2012, replacement of the Common Agricultural Policy with support for local food markets, a complete ban on genetically modified food, and measures to tackle anti-competitive supermarket behaviour.

## Crime and Justice

Crime reduction focuses on community strengthening, improved urban design, and addressing social causes of crime. The party supports increased community policing, tough gun control legislation, and restorative justice programmes. They strongly oppose national ID cards.

## Democratic Reform

Constitutional reforms include proportional representation for Westminster and local government, an elected House of Lords, devolution of power to regions, and a written constitution. The party campaigns against the proposed EU constitution while supporting continued EU membership with reforms.

## International Policy

The manifesto advocates withdrawal from Iraq, nuclear disarmament, reducing military spending to the EU average, and increasing overseas aid to 1% of Gross National Investment. The Greens support cancelling debt for the 52 poorest countries, reforming the UN Security Council, and replacing WTO rules with a General Agreement on Sustainable Trade favouring local economies.
